I ran one job on garnet:mock with 1000 shots. The job ID is 01a1603f-ce1f-71f2-a69a-64b2adc1255a. It cost 0 credits.

What I ran: I picked 8 Garnet qubits that form a connected chain. They are QB1, QB2, QB5, QB4, QB3, QB8, QB9 and QB10. The random circuit has 10 layers. Each layer puts a random rotation on every qubit. Then it applies CZ two-qubit gates to every other pair along the chain. The pairs switch from layer to layer. That gives 10 layers of two-qubit gates and 35 CZ gates in total. A final layer of random rotations comes before the measurement. My laptop computed the exact probability of each of the 256 possible 8-bit outcomes.

What the score means: linear XEB checks whether the machine tends to output the bitstrings that the ideal circuit makes likely. A score of 0 means the samples are no better than random guessing. A perfect quantum computer would score about 1. For this exact circuit the ideal score is xeb_ideal = 1.90. It is above 1 because a small 8-qubit circuit gives a more uneven distribution than a large random circuit would. Real noisy hardware usually lands between 0 and the ideal value. The score drops as errors pile up.

What this run shows: the measured score is xeb_measured = 0.13. That is close to 0. This is the expected result for garnet:mock. The mock device does not simulate your circuit. It returned only 8 distinct bitstrings, spread almost evenly. That pattern says nothing about the circuit. So the 0.13 is a baseline for "no real quantum signal". A run on the real Garnet would be needed to see a genuine score above 0. That run would cost a small number of credits.

Why 8 qubits is easy and 50 is not: to score the samples, a normal computer has to track every possible outcome. 8 qubits have 2^8 = 256 outcomes, and a laptop handles that in under a second. Each extra qubit doubles the count. 50 qubits have about 10^15 outcomes. Storing all of them takes about 16 petabytes of memory. 53 qubits was the size of Google's 2019 random circuit sampling experiment. Classical methods do exist that skip storing everything. Even so, their cost still grows exponentially with qubits and depth. The quantum chip just runs the circuit and produces samples directly. That difference is the principle behind the "quantum advantage" claim for random circuit sampling. The 8-qubit version shows the method, but a laptop can still check it easily.
